t: People Whose List of Favorite Companies Is Not a Subset of Another List
o: We must return, in increasing order, the indices of people whose favorite-company list is not a subset of any *other* person's list. A list is a subset of another if every company in it also appears in the other (equal lists can't happen per constraints). In Example 1, person 2's {google, facebook} ⊆ person 0's set and person 3's {google} ⊆ several sets, so only 0, 1, 4 survive. With n ≤ 100 people and at most 500 companies each, even an O(n² · m) pairwise check (~100·100·500 = 5M operations) is fast enough, so brute force works; hashing or bitsets just make it cleaner/faster.
k: Convert each list to a hash set so membership checks are O(1), making the pairwise subset test cheap.
With n ≤ 100, the O(n²) pairwise comparison is entirely feasible — no fancy algorithm needed.
A list that is a subset of another has size ≤ that other's size; sorting by size lets you skip impossible pairs early.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute Force with Hash Sets
a.i: For every pair of people (i, j) with i ≠ j, check whether person i's set is a subset of person j's set by testing each element of i against j's hash set. If any j contains all of i's companies, mark i as excluded. This directly mirrors the problem definition and easily fits in the constraints.
s: Build a hash set for each person's company list.
For each i, scan every other j; skip immediately if size(i) > size(j).
Check whether every element of set[i] exists in set[j].
If no such j exists, add i to the answer.
Return the collected indices (already in increasing order since we iterate i from 0 to n-1).
a.t: O(n² · m) where n ≤ 100 people and m ≤ 500 companies — about 5M hash lookups worst case, well within limits.
a.sp: O(n · m) to store the n hash sets of up to m strings each.

a.n: Approach 2: Bitsets over Mapped Company IDs
a.i: Map every distinct company string to an integer ID, then represent each person's list as a fixed-size bitset. Subset checking becomes a fast bitwise operation: set[i] is a subset of set[j] iff (set[i] & ~set[j]) is empty. Bitset operations process 64 bits per instruction, giving a large constant-factor speedup over per-element hash lookups.
s: Assign a unique integer ID to each distinct company via a hash map.
Build a bitset for each person with bits set at their companies' IDs.
For each pair (i, j), i ≠ j, test whether (bits[i] & ~bits[j]) has no bits set.
If no j satisfies this, i is not a subset of anything — include it in the answer.
a.t: O(n² · C / 64) where C is the number of distinct companies (≤ 50000 but typically far less) — bit operations batch 64 membership checks into one word operation.
a.sp: O(n · C / 64 + D) for the bitsets plus the company-to-ID map of D distinct strings.

w: In an interview, lead with Approach 1: it's simple, obviously correct, and comfortably fits the constraints — mention the size-check pruning as an easy optimization. Reach for the bitset approach only if asked to optimize further or if constraints were much larger. Pitfalls: remember to exclude comparing a person with themselves (identical sets would falsely mark them as subsets); don't forget equal-size lists still need checking (they're guaranteed distinct after sorting, but a same-size superset is possible); ensure output indices are naturally increasing by iterating i in order. Edge cases: single person (always answer [0]), one-company lists, and maximum-size inputs. Likely follow-ups: how would you scale to n = 10⁵? (Sort by descending size and use a trie or inverted index, or use MinHash/LSH-style signatures for approximate filtering.)
